Jeannie and Jimmy Cheatham

Jeannie and Jimmy Cheatham have been creating swinging blues together since the late 50s, when they met in Buffalo, New York. Jimmy has played trombone with Duke Ellington, Lionel Hampton and Ornette Coleman, and taught jazz at Bennington College, the University of Wisconsin, and at the University of California at San Diego. His arrangements for the Sweet Baby Blues Band capture the Kansas City jump blues style and make the seven-piece band swing like Jay McShann and Count Basie.

Jeannie started as a classical piano student, but found a new sound to pursue after hearing Charlie Parker and Lester Young. She has accompanied Joe Williams, Big Mama Thornton and T-Bone Walker, and she was featured in the film “Three Generations of Blues” with Sippie Wallace and Ms. Thornton. This production was inducted into the Library of Congress’ 1997 Jazz Film Series along with the film, “Jeannie & Jimmy Cheatham and the Sweet Baby Blues Band.” They continue to add to their list of accomplishments from their home base in San Diego.
Jeannie and Jimmy were interviewed in San Diego, California on February 12, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

We are filming today in San Diego for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. And I’m really thrilled to have today as our guests, Jeannie and Jimmy Cheatham, masters of the blues, and educators. And I wanted to tell you something that happened to me on the way out here. Before I got on the plane in Syracuse I was listening to some of your records. So all the way on the plane, all seven hours, I had this, “Baby, meet me with your black drawers on.” That was in my head, all the way out here.
Imagine us doing that to ya.
And you know that’s the mark of a great tune.
It is.
If it sticks with you like that.
That’s it, man.
How did you guys come up with that?
It’s whistleable.

It just sort of came out. You know we were working on that first album, and we were just fooling around, and when we went in the studio, it was after the session was over, then we just went into — there was no arrangement or anything. And so we never dreamed they would ever put it on the record.
Strictly head. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
We did it for fun. And so we thought it would be against the law or something. But they put it on the record.
Yeah, we thought they’d ban it. We were so surprised.
We were really shocked that it came out you know.
I really like the end too, you said — remember what you said at the end?
That’s Snooky.
That’s Snooky.
Snooky blamed Jimmy for a long time.
He blamed me, see, all the time.
He didn’t want his wife to know that he was there.

He didn’t want his wife to know that he said that, see? You know, so we had to cool it for a while, then all of a sudden, he got to liking it you know. So the next session, he became the director again —
Of the Glee Club.
Of the Glee Club, see?
Yeah, he’s the official director.
Yeah, official director.
Well for some of our maybe — students that will watch this later on, you said you know, that was a head arrangement.
Yeah, totally.
Could you just, in your own words, explain about the head arrangement? Because that’s a bit of a lost art these days.

Oh, yeah. Well one of the main reasons is due to the times, you know, because coming up in our era, and all the perennial giants who set the pace for everything you know, they did a lot of head playing, and specifically noted for that was the Kansas City style see? That’s why we refer to the Kansas City style. In other words, riffs, tunes, and you make up a tune and you take it until you decide to—
To stop.

To stop. It could be all night. Really. Depends on the groove you know and everything. And so in other words, it just comes immediately, it’s an improvisation right from — a spontaneous phrase right from the get-go, you know, from the head. And everybody’s just tuning in to each other you know. While one is playing the lead, another will set up a tune, and they listen to it and make a little background to it or something like that. Or they’ll pick up the tune as a total unison thing, and make it a big mass unison, and then go into solos and then riffs and things like that.
And then it might get written down later.
Oh, yeah, later. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Yeah, especially if they like it. I think also that it’s best to be taken from like Gospel or spiritual music you know? Because you always have a lead singer, or the preacher, he’s doing his thing and everybody’s saying “Amen.” And then the preacher goes from the one to the third to the fifth to the seventh. And when he hits the seventh he’s ready to take everybody out.
Yeah. That’s how you get this going.

Yeah, I noted that even when I was little. And so whoever is playing the solo is the preacher for the moment. And everybody else is doing “Amen.” And then the next soloist takes over, and he’s the preacher for the moment, and everybody else says the “Amen.” So it’s really that simple.
Really.
But you’ve got to live it.
He’d follow — and soloists would follow that, would actually follow that format, in terms like she was saying, tonic, third, fifth, seventh. That’s why each chorus —
Sort of grows.
Grows.
And it changes.
In other words you become aware of building. Like creativity. Like the law of creativity dictates that. In terms of the energy. Energizing.
And when you got up to that seventh, that just kind of had to resolve eventually?
Eventually.
Eventually. Sometimes you’d just leave it hanging you see? So that’s why you start having dominant chord endings, see?
Oh. Come back next week and we’ll find it.
We’ll find it.
Well you guys met on stage in the 50s? Now I read this and I want to know if it’s true.
It’s pretty much true.
Yeah, very much so, yeah. It was like a quick — she got a quick call I found out later, I had no idea she would be there and vice versa.
From the president of the union.
In Buffalo.
In Buffalo. Because we had come in from Toronto with our group to do the jam session, that went on all night long, one Sunday, at the musician’s club.
At the musician’s club, upstairs see?
And so the president said, “Jeannie, they need a piano player in there” what was that, the Elks or somewhere.
That was at — yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
I think it was the Elks Club.
Yeah, it was the Elks up on the—
An Elks Club?

He said, “Would you go and play over there?” And I said, “This is my day off, I don’t want to play the Elks.” And he said, “Please,” he said, “just do me a favor.” And so when I came in there there was all these guys and then, really older guys, and so I knew they were going to play “Honeysuckle Rose”—
Yeah, you know, the standards.
Right.
“Take the A Train,” and whatever, so I said that would be an easy gig. And then Jimmy came in. And he was a younger guy.
I was the second youngest next to her.
Next to me, right. And so I said oh, wait a minute. So you know, all the musicians like put a dollar in a pile and we’d always get a bottle so we didn’t have to buy it.
Yeah.

So that way, after the gig we used to sit around and tell tales you know. So I put my dollar in. And after the gig I looked around and I was going to talk to this guy — he had gone. He cut out. I didn’t see him for three more years.
That’s right.
Really? That was almost the end right there.
Well almost.

And I had just come back from California, not too long beforehand. And so that was kind of a habitual thing. After the gig was over and the pack up, and as Papa Jo Jones would say, “With our mutual armies we’ll move out smiling.”

But I was always hanging around because I liked the stories. See because he had more of an advantage in that he had a chance to grow up listening to people and talking to people like Jo Jones and Ben Webster—
And Lester Young.
And Lester Young and all these people, because they were in the service with him.
Yeah. Chico Hamilton and — I slept in the top bunk and Chico slept on the bottom you see?

And I hadn’t had that experience at all, because I stayed mostly up in Canada and in the middle part of the country where we played mostly. So I hadn’t had a chance to meet any of the big guys like that.
She played a lot for those big singers — all the top singers.
I know, but that was later. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
Let me ask you about that in a moment. I wanted to ask you, at that time when you had first met, was there still a black musician’s and a white musician’s union?
Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. You see but I was part of the integration in Hollywood, see? Because I had finished school at the Westlake College of Music in Hollywood for film scoring and radio and T.V. and all of that, after I had finished the New York Conservatory of Modern Music in Brooklyn you see. And it was in that particular sojourn, and going to Hollywood for that, it’s where I also challenged the Local 47, the white local, why they refused my card. I said well why can’t I, as a transfer person, transfer it, and also become a member in due time, according to the rules and regulations? And they said well no, we can’t accept you you know. So anyway, long story short, I had the Dr. Lernard, who was the director of the school, I went back and told him, because the school was right there on Vine and Yukon, in Hollywood, see. And so my whole reason was look, I’m here, in Hollywood, every day. And so Local 767, which is the black local, was way over on the east side you see, on Central Avenue. And so anyway, Dr. Lernard set up an appointment and we discussed it and everything. So we went through a whole lot of politics and everything. So anyway, the only satisfaction was that I brought them to admit, that the only reason why they wouldn’t accept me was due to a gentleman’s agreement. I knew they understood that, because I got that from high school. So I knew how to relate to them when it came to that. So I said well okay, I’ll be back. And before I left, sure enough they had a caucus and got together and the unions merged, and the same people were in office, because they stay in office a pretty long time, ‘til they die you know. And so when they came over to the 767 to make the graces and everything about the unions coming together, and be an amalgamated, see that was the word that was used, amalgamation — not integration or anything like that — amalgamation.
Mmm. There’s a thought.
That was the word. And well that was due to the ACLU.
I see.
It was a powerful move, believe me.
And that year was—
This was like 195—— late 50s — like middle ‘53. Actually it was going on say from ‘52, ‘52 and then ‘53 when that finally happened — when it finally happened like in ‘53, late ‘53 or early ‘54.
Did you both know you were going to be musicians at a young age?
Yes. I did.
Let me ask you first. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

I did. I knew that. I wanted to be an artist, but I started taking lessons very early, five, six years old, from a very good teacher from England, his name was Arthur Reginald Riley. And he was a very good teacher. I learned to play classical music and read everything and plus I played in church you see. So it was a very — it didn’t seem unnatural for me. I knew that that was my life’s work at a very early age. It was either that or be a school teacher and I knew I didn’t want to be a school teacher.
I think we’re glad that you went the music route.
I am. Definitely.
There’s nothing wrong with being a school teacher.
Oh, it’s an honorable profession.
It better be honorable because it don’t pay. So you might as well be a — what you love doing — be a jazz musician and starve to death too.
That’s right, there’s some similarities there.
Take a vow of poverty.
That’s it.
How about yourself? Was trombone your first instrument?

Actually baritone horn was my first instrument, in terms of performing on it, because my arm wasn’t long enough to reach all the way out to the seventh position on the trombone, slide trombone you know. So the music instructor kind of smiled and says, “Look, see, you know you’ve got to grow a little more, to really deal with the horn.” He says, “So if you don’t mind me making a suggestion, how about playing a baritone horn?” I said, you know, okay. I wanted to get started you see. And so I stayed with the baritone horn for like the first year. And this was in grade school. And the following year, which was like seventh grade — I started in sixth grade — then I stayed with the baritone in seventh and then in eighth grade I went to the trombone you see. And made the orchestra and all that. But my first involvment in music performance was voice. I sang — I was also appointed as one of the members of the Hundred Voice Choir, a city boy choir in the city, all-city. And so I sang in the choir and also a solo. So that got me performing personally.
And you learned to read music at that age, and the whole thing.
Oh yeah, yeah.

That shows you the difference in the school system, and also the city system. Because we had the same thing, everybody took music. It was a requirement. And they used to have like spring festivals and things, where your group from this school would go against this one, and you’d find the all-Ohio singers and they’d come and take the best out of everyone.
That’s how it happened, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Just like sports. And the May festivals. And gee I played vocal choir, orchestra, they were doing musicals, and so we had to play for those people and they would put on a show every year. And this all in grade school mind you. And we still were taking math and everything else that we had to take.
But it was equally required.
It was just required, just like sports.

And right into high school. Because I played in the jazz band in high school, the orchestra, and also the marching band, and the marching band was the same as the pep band. Today they have the pep band and marching band, but at that time the marching band did both jobs. Because after the first year, in terms of my sophomore year, I actually went into playing football you see. But I was still playing in the orchestra, but I couldn’t play in the marching band because like trying to be in two places at one time.
Well that would have been a good one, because you’d be flying over the stadium.

And you know it was so beautiful, the instructors were fantastic. I mean they had depth, breath and height, and I know you know what I’m talking about, as a human being, trained to transmit knowledge.
So much more than just the music, right?
Oh, yeah. It was like a life thing.

And that’s where I became — it struck a chord here. And that’s it, I said I knew what I wanted to do. Which actually it was an affirmation really, and a confirmation. Because at home, before even getting into school, when I was like four and five years old — two and say three, after — I was born in Birmingham, Alabama but I came there when I was about three years old, two and a half to three years. But anyway, my uncle, in Buffalo, New York, had all the records. And the word — I didn’t know it then, but — he was looking back, he was a very eclectic — he had a very eclectic ear. He had from country, spirituals, to opera, Lawrence Tibbett and I always recall her name, but Lily Pons. You know that’s going back you know.
You never thought you’d say that, did you?
No, no. Because I’m watching his eyes. And naturally Caruso you see. And just name it, I heard all these, all this. And then we had the piano at the house—
Everybody had a piano at that time. Everybody had a piano.
Yeah, at that time. It’s like everybody in the south had an organ way back earlier, you know what I mean? Had a little pump organ.
And now they’ve just begun to gather data about what that does to a child’s spatial knowledge by — it has to do with music.
That’s right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
And I’m not going out of here without them knowing that. Because we’ve said it for years, and so we’ve lived it.
And our structures, that’s why you heard me say that — I didn’t know you hadn’t heard that, three dimensions, depth, breadth and height. Because you’re dealing with a pyramid there.

I’m going to pause for one second—This curtain was too close and it’s rubbing the back of your head. You okay? So we’ll just pick up, we’ll edit that out. That’s so true with the education and sometimes I see kids who have a really hard time even clapping or moving to a beat. And I’m going, why is that? I want to know why that is. And I suspect it’s because they don’t have music in the house.
Oh, yeah.
Exactly.
It doesn’t sink in.

Because it’s like we’re more mass conscious I would say as of now, we’re becoming much more aware of being aware of the power of music. Because what it can do subliminally, without any overt influences, is amazing. We haven’t gotten to that yet.

Well then do you feel that the negative influence is also possible? I mean there’s a kind of controversy about a lot of the music that’s out today, whether it be rap or heavy metal — some of the things that they’re saying — if music can be a positive influence, can it also go the other way?

I don’t really know. All I know is that some of the studies that I’ve been following find that the more simple, the simpler the music is, the more the child learns, even in utero. Like just a plain little chord — a 1-3-5 chord and maybe a 7th you know, later. And the simpler the music is, it seems to widen their spatial sense. And then they also find that vocal music also. But it has to be a certain type, simple again you see. So I have a feeling that they’re going to find that each one of the chords have a power and really correspond to a part of the person’s brain and body. So I’m thinking that pretty soon — they can measure this stuff now, I know they can.
In terms of brain waves.
See I know they can. And I’m quite sure that the powers that be, that keep saying that we don’t need music in the schools —
That’s the negative part.

That’s more negative than rap, and I like rap on certain things, because they have a lot of people that teach very interesting things through rap. And the rhythm of the words is a power in itself. It’s almost like haiku poetry if you want to talk about. Because that’s in a sense, an art form in itself. One day we’re going to probably peel away a couple of verses and things and say, oh this is really poetry, it’s wonderful poetry. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Another interesting thing, not to oversimplify, but to me it’s like getting right into the source, like looking into the sun but not too long because you can become blind as a bat. But the thing is is that we look at sound. Sound does not happen unless it has a vibrating body in some way, shape, form or fashion. But sound itself, the nature of sound, is emanated from a vibration. There is nothing that exists on this planet earth or in its environment or the universe that doesn’t have, is not affected by vibration. The sun rays. How many miles — they say how many million miles, 83 million or something like that? But nobody’s got that close to find out about it. But the point is, by even projecting that, you know that you feel the vibration of that heat. You follow me? And so that has to have, without a doubt, whatever, knowingly or unknowingly, some aspect of effect from a scientific point of view, on every living thing on this planet. Man.
We’ll have to sit and analyze that.

Well sure. But you know, Count Basie’s music, and for some reason a lot of the people that call them connoisseurs or want to write all about music, for some reason they sort of leave him over here. And they’re always talking about somebody else over here. But he knew exactly how to maintain order. He played his music and it corresponded to the heart beat. And he knew that. He was born to do that. He was one of the best at that, if you want to speak of something that he contributed. He really knew how to move and make a crowd feel wonderful because he never, he put that music right there, where it belonged, in the heartbeat.

And the most beautiful thing, hearing a thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, now seventeen piece band — or five, etcetera — at the time it was smaller. When he’d say “bing” — look out. And the band would say — oh.
What power that was.
It’s amazing. Now that’s understood.

That’s what I relate to my students. Just last night I had my rehearsal, on Tuesday and Wednesday nights, and every time we go through things, at the end of the chart, and I made them aware that if I say it over and over, in many different ways, about, I say believe me, music is powerful. I don’t say jazz is powerful. I say music is powerful. Whatever its form or style is, and wherever it’s coming from on this planet or anywhere else, in terms of the way to deal with the music of the spirits and try that. But the thing is, we haven’t begun to even — we’re just scratching the surface.
When they say harmony, you know we used to go to like an arranger’s band in Buffalo, New York, where people could bring in different arrangements and we’d rehearse. And then we’d put on a big show.
We’d put on a showcase. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

A showcase once a month. And we had this one guy, he would come in with these arrangements, and he would pass out the music, and everybody’s feeling great. And he’d bring his hand down, and the band would fight — start this big fight. Believe me.
That first chord.
The first chord.
And all of a sudden everybody’s like [growls].
Everybody yells, and punches, and they’d head for the bar and double Gugenheimer — you remember that?
Yeah, the Gugenheimer whiskey, that was a special at the club.

And Jimmy and I would watch this thing. I said, it was consistent. I said I don’t care what he writes, every time he writes something, everybody starts fighting. See it’s so much cacophony and so many notes.
And see that gnarling vibration see, all it matters is that it makes your nerve system catch a good hold of that, and he’d be sitting back like this.
Watching the set.
Oh, he liked it.
He was aware of what he was doing. So when you spoke earlier, we could go around the track about the negative aspect you see.
There you go.

Oh yes, yes. And you know just like in anything else. Just like the church. You’ve got the minister and it could be positive or he could be very negative at times, in the sense of power and controlling, from that point of view and that type of stuff. So it’s always AC/DC, just like in terms of electricity. You’ve got to have a little negative and a little positive power in order to have a good pole of electricity.
Well that’s what — among the things I love about the blues is that you can play the quote wrong notes, the blue notes, that clash theoretically, but that they still sound so good.
Because they’re bent.
Because they’re bent.
Yeah. They never go straight on.

And the other reason is because of dealing with the system in terms of the western world, we scientifically divided everything up. There’s nothing wrong with that. But to make that the total aspect of what music is about, is where the negative aspect of conveying that message you see. When it came to opera, I mean [inaudible] — they didn’t know anything about China. And anything that sounded strange, they would say it’s Chinese music. But they’re in deep trouble now you see. Globally, they’re in deep trouble. All of a sudden they find out there’s other people living elsewhere. And they have their respective cultures according to the creative process that we live in. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Pentatonic scales.
And how does that fit in? How are we going to resolve that with our own eight note scale?

Well the whole thing is we’re coming, see we come to grips with that because, again, when we speak in terms of poverty, at least from my point of view I like to look at the aspect of creation. You’re dealing with such a fine sense, I say we are vibration — balance. And so we can go to China and say, or Japan and say yin yang, or wherever it is, they’ve got a word for balance you see. And music speaks strongly to the nature of what we all are about in terms of the creative process. And we have a choice how we wish to use it in terms of our given talents.
Well said. Wow. Let me ask you about some things from years past. You had some big band experience along the way, with some of our more notable big band leaders.
Very fortunate, yeah.
If you had to pick a time that was one of your favorites in one of those bands, what might it be?
Well I can’t say favorites. Each one, in terms of the experience, what it offered me, was that same, like I say aspect of being uplifted.
There’s nothing like a big band.

And maintaining an open mind you see. Now sure I could talk about being on the road, and the negative hassles, and etcetera. But the amazing thing about it all, because you’re still sleeping and whatnot you know, and eating with the individuals, was on that bandstand.
Nothing like it. It’s worth everything.

Everything became one. And there’s all this diverse expression coming out of these horns. And from one section to the next, speaking to each other. Then in terms of mass unisons and you know, whatever, and solos, personal expression. And that whole band, just like when you hear Basie, it speaks.
And it was different when he was with Duke.
Duke Ellington.
And Maynard Ferguson. I really liked hanging around with that group. They were really hip.
Was that the small big band with Maynard, or was it a whole—

No actually it was a big band. It was a time that he and what’s his name, that was traveling with him then that was on the road together. He and Maynard would take this chemical or whatever it was. And they would stay out of their minds you know. But the thing is — I can’t think of his name right now.
Yeah, well you probably better not. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

But all I’m saying, the important thing is that, I mean this was a highly intellectual man. This was no, you know, peddler or anything like that. I mean he was highly respected as a human being. But that was the only time they were traveling on the road together. Willie Maiden was the straw boss. That’s how I got in the band, because Willie Maiden and I finished Westlake College of Music together in Hollywood you see. And he called me up, they were on their way — in fact they were coming to Buffalo to play a gig, and he had found out that I was in Buffalo. And the trombone player had to go home to bury his dad in Texas. So he called me up and said, “Hey man, I’d like for you to come on over to this club we’re playing and make this gig with us, because we don’t want to show up short a man, because our contract could be voided.”
Yeah. Then they don’t want to pay you.

So at that time we had our jazz showcase going on and I was doing a lot of writing and stuff like that. I said, “Well I haven’t been playing too much, really.” We’d been doing a lot of writing and stuff, and he says, “Look Jim” he says, “I know about you. Please do me that favor.” And I talked with Jeannie, and she says, “Hey, go ahead.” And so I made it. And so I went out to that club that night, and walked in and we sat down. And I had met Maynard before, in Hollywood see. And so when we got ready to hit, I said well here it goes, and where it stops nobody knows, but I’m going to give it the best shot, and everybody’s falling out laughing.
He had some great young trumpet players.
Yeah.
And some hard arrangements too.
Wooo, yeah. He had this lead trumpet player, who was also a fine educator too. And he was just a wonderful —
And Speedy was on the drums.
And Speedy Jones was playing the drums, and Jackie Byard was playing piano.
It was a good band.
So the rhythm section was — a really good band you know, a fantastic band. And we had a lot of fun.
I like big bands. That’s sort of my first experience in jazz.

That’s a powerful experience you know. But I think all the youngsters, if they have an opportunity if they play in the marching band or whatever, have an opportunity to play some big band music, you know, it’s on another level. Even a good strong marching band is a heck of a level too. There’s a heck of a high you know. Or a concert band is a heck of a high. But then you get into a jazz band and it’s like whew.
There’s another level there. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Another level. And they all have their levels. That’s why I said to try to say which is my favorite, is very difficult for me, because they’re all very — for me anyway — very positive. I accept everything that went with it, because that’s what made it positive you see.
And that’s the only way you can hang out.
It’s the only way.
To be a musician you have to be, I think, super flexible. Because otherwise, how could you make it at all?

And also that coincides with, even though they coined that phrase “jazz” and they refer to “improvisation,” — the act of improving on something, right, improvisation, that’s what it is. That’s what I explain to my kids you see. I say everybody does that on this planet. Nobody knows everything. So living life is a total improvisational experience. And those who are trying to fix it so it’s like one-two-three, eventually find out it doesn’t work one- two-three all the time. They’ve got to deal with the law of permutation.
Do you find that some of your students have more success simply because of their personalities? That they’re more easy going or willing to take chances?
I think so.
Yeah, yeah. Well because that’s that freedom we speak about in terms of personal expression again you see.
You have to be fearless.
Yes, yes.
And that comes from having confidence.
Really.

And I think — I don’t think you could teach anybody that. I think a lot of their early life experiences with their folks and maybe even before they’re born, I think there’s a heck of a lot to even deal with that. Because most real fearful people, they can accomplish a lot in another direction, but I don’t think they can be a musician. Not a jazz musician, and be that fearful. It has something also to do with faith.
That’s it.

Like someplace, somewhere, somebody needs a good band? Because you just have to feel like tomorrow’s going to be okay.
